mcq.q: Partner Kavita advanced ₹2,00,000 to the firm, beyond her capital, on 1 July. The deed is silent on interest. Under Section 13(d), the interest due to her for the year ending 31 March is:
options: Nil
mcq.explain: Section 13(d) gives a partner who advances money to the firm beyond his agreed capital interest at 6% per annum, unless the partners agree otherwise. From 1 July to 31 March is 9 months, so interest = ₹2,00,000 × 6% × 9/12 = ₹9,000. Interest on capital, by contrast, is not payable unless agreed.
mcq.topic: Relation of partners to one another (Sections 9 to 15)
mcq.fast: Advance (not capital) = 6% p.a. by default; count the months.

mcq.q: The partnership deed is silent about interest on capital. The partners are entitled to:
options: Interest at 6% p.a. on capital
No interest on capital
Interest at the bank rate
Interest at 12% p.a. on capital
mcq.explain: Under Section 13(c), a partner is not entitled to interest on capital unless the partners have agreed to pay it, and even then it is payable only out of profits. The 6% default rate in Section 13(d) applies only to advances made beyond the agreed capital, not to capital itself.
mcq.topic: Relation of partners to one another (Sections 9 to 15)
mcq.fast: Capital = no interest unless agreed. Advance = 6%.

mcq.q: In the absence of any agreement, profits and losses of a firm are shared by partners:
options: In the ratio of their capitals
In the ratio of the time they devote
Equally — Section 13(b)
As decided by the senior partner
mcq.explain: Section 13(b): unless the partners agree otherwise, profits are divided equally and losses are borne equally, even if one partner brought in much more capital than the others. Capital contributed or time spent does not change this unless the partners have agreed otherwise.
mcq.topic: Relation of partners to one another (Sections 9 to 15)
mcq.fast: No agreement = equal sharing, whatever the capital.

mcq.q: Which act is within a partner's implied authority, in a trading firm, without any special usage?
options: Buying goods of the kind the firm deals in, in the usual way
Opening a bank account for the firm in his own name
Submitting a dispute of the firm to arbitration
Buying immovable property for the firm
mcq.explain: Under Section 19(1) a partner's act done to carry on the firm's business in the usual way binds the firm, so buying stock-in-trade is within implied authority. Section 19(2) lists acts outside implied authority unless usage permits: arbitration, opening a bank account in his own name, compromising claims, and acquiring or transferring immovable property, among others.
mcq.topic: Partner as agent: implied authority and its limits (Sections 18 to 22)
mcq.fast: Ordinary trade purchases = yes. Anything on the s.19(2) list (arbitration, own-name bank account, land) = no.

mcq.q: For the firm's obligations incurred during his membership, each partner is liable:
options: Only in proportion to their capital
Jointly with all the other partners and also severally — Section 25
Only up to their share of profits
Only if they personally signed the contract
mcq.explain: Section 25 makes each partner answerable, together with the others and also individually, for every act of the firm during his time as partner. A creditor can therefore recover the whole debt from any one partner, who may then seek contribution from the others. There is no limited liability in an ordinary firm.
mcq.fast: Firm debts: each partner can be made to pay the whole (joint and several).

mcq.q: Gopal is not a partner, but at a meeting he lets Harish describe him as a partner of Harish & Co. Relying on this, a supplier gives the firm credit. Gopal is:
options: Liable to the supplier as if he were a partner — Section 28
Not liable, since he is not a partner
Liable only if he signed the order
Liable only for half the debt
mcq.explain: Section 28 treats a person who holds himself out as a partner, or knowingly allows others to do so, as a partner towards anyone who extends credit to the firm relying on that impression. This is liability by holding out, or estoppel.
mcq.fast: Let others call you a partner + creditor relied on it = liable (holding out).

mcq.q: Raju, who was let into the benefits of a firm while a minor, turns 18 and stays silent, issuing no public notice for six months. He:
options: Automatically ceases to be connected with the firm
Becomes a partner and is personally liable for all acts of the firm since his admission to benefits
Becomes a partner liable only for acts after majority
Remains a minor partner indefinitely
mcq.explain: Section 30 gives the minor six months after attaining majority, or after learning of his admission if later, to give public notice of his choice. Silence for those six months makes him a full partner, and he then answers personally to outsiders for everything the firm did right from the date he was first given its benefits.
mcq.topic: Minors admitted to the benefits of partnership (Section 30)
mcq.fast: Silent for 6 months = partner, liable from the day of admission to benefits.

mcq.q: A new partner can be admitted into an existing firm, unless the contract provides otherwise:
options: Only if every existing partner agrees — Section 31
With the consent of a majority of partners
By the senior partner alone
By any partner
mcq.explain: Section 31: subject to any contrary agreement and the special rule for minors, a newcomer joins only if every existing partner agrees; a single objecting partner can block the admission. Partnership rests on mutual trust, so every partner gets a veto.
mcq.topic: Partner coming in and going out (Sections 31 to 35)

mcq.q: Partner Dinesh dies in June. In August, without any public notice, the surviving partners buy goods on credit in the firm's name. Is Dinesh's estate liable for this debt?
options: Yes — until public notice of his death is given
No — a dead partner's estate is free from the firm's later acts (Section 35)
Yes — but only up to his capital
Yes — jointly with the surviving partners
mcq.explain: Under Section 35, when the business carries on after a partner dies, his estate bears no liability for what the firm does afterwards. Unlike retirement, no public notice is needed, because death is itself treated as notice to the world. The surviving partners alone are liable for the August purchases.
mcq.topic: Partner coming in and going out (Sections 31 to 35)
mcq.fast: Death = no public notice needed; estate free for later acts. Retirement = public notice needed.

mcq.q: Partner Rohit retires; his share of ₹5,00,000 is not settled and the others continue the business for one year. If he opts for interest instead of a share of profits, under Section 37 he gets:
mcq.explain: Section 37 lets an outgoing partner, whose share is not settled and whose firm continues using his property, claim either the share of profits attributable to the use of his share, or interest at 6% per annum on it, at his option. Interest = ₹5,00,000 × 6% × 1 year = ₹30,000.
mcq.topic: Outgoing partner: competing business, subsequent profits, guarantees (Sections 36 to 38)
mcq.fast: Outgoing partner: profits on his share OR 6% interest — his choice.

mcq.q: In a firm of five partners, three want to change the firm's business from textiles to real estate. The other two object. Under Section 12(c):
options: The majority decision prevails
The senior-most partner decides
The change cannot be made without the consent of all partners
The change can be made if the three partners hold most of the capital
mcq.explain: Section 12(c) lets the majority settle routine business disagreements, but altering what kind of business the firm does needs every partner's agreement, so the two objectors can block the change. Moving from textiles to real estate changes the nature of the business.
mcq.topic: Relation of partners to one another (Sections 9 to 15)
mcq.fast: Ordinary matters = majority; change in NATURE of business = all.
